title: Air India and IndiGo Are Slashing Summer Domestic Flights — and NRIs Will Feel It on the Last Leg Home
excerpt: A 22 per cent cut at Air India and 7 per cent at IndiGo means fewer connections, higher fares, and tighter rebooking options for the millions heading to India this summer.
body:
Air India will slash domestic flights by 22 per cent in June and July, and IndiGo will trim its own schedule by up to 7 per cent, as both carriers buckle under jet fuel prices that have surged in the wake of the Iran conflict. For the roughly 4.5 million Indian Americans who fly to India each year — and then connect onward to tier-2 cities — the cuts will land squarely on the last mile of their journey home.

What's happening

Air India confirmed on Tuesday that it had "temporarily rationalised operations on certain domestic routes" from June through August, citing "the sustained impact of high fuel prices on overall operations." A person familiar with the carrier's plans told Reuters the June-July reductions amount to 22 per cent of its domestic schedule. August cuts are still being finalised.

IndiGo, which controls 63.3 per cent of the domestic market, is pulling back 5 to 7 per cent of capacity over the same window. Together, the two airlines account for nearly 90 per cent of India's domestic traffic.

The affected routes include some of the busiest corridors NRIs use after landing at a hub: Mumbai–Ahmedabad, Delhi–Hyderabad, Bengaluru–Chennai, and Delhi–Lucknow. Fares on surviving flights are already climbing — the combination of fewer seats and steady demand is textbook pricing pressure.

Why it matters for NRIs

If you land at Delhi or Mumbai on a nonstop from the US and have a connecting domestic flight, your margin for error just shrank. Fewer frequencies mean fewer rebooking options if your international leg is delayed. And for NRIs heading to smaller cities — Coimbatore, Ranchi, Patna, Vizag — the cuts disproportionately hit thinner routes that already had limited service.

The timing is particularly painful. June and July are peak NRI travel months: summer breaks, weddings, family visits. Air India logged an annual loss exceeding $2 billion, battered not just by fuel but by Pakistan's continuing airspace ban on Indian carriers (which forces longer routings on some domestic-to-international connections) and a strong US dollar that inflates rupee-denominated costs.

The fuel backdrop

Aviation turbine fuel prices have jumped roughly 25 per cent since the escalation of hostilities near the Strait of Hormuz, and Indian ATF carries one of the world's highest tax burdens. Delhi and Maharashtra recently cut their VAT on jet fuel to 7 per cent each — a welcome step, but one that barely dents the cumulative surge. IndiGo has already revised its fuel surcharge upward, and analysts expect another round before monsoon season peaks.

Meanwhile, Akasa Air, the Rakesh Jhunjhunwala-founded newcomer, is expanding into the gaps — adding routes and capacity where the incumbents are pulling back. For NRIs flexible on carrier, Akasa may become a viable domestic connector this summer.

What to do

Book domestic connections early — same-day availability on popular routes will be scarce. Consider building in an overnight stay at your hub city rather than relying on a tight connection. And watch for Akasa and SpiceJet picking up routes the big two have dropped. Train travel is also getting a serious upgrade: India's new Vande Bharat sleeper services now cover corridors like Howrah–Guwahati, and a Mumbai–Bengaluru overnight service is imminent.

The carriers say they will "restore frequencies as conditions stabilise." Translation: when oil prices drop. NRIs planning summer trips should not count on that happening before August.
nri_angle: NRIs connecting through Delhi and Mumbai to tier-2 cities face fewer domestic flights, higher fares, and shrinking rebooking options during peak summer travel months.
author: Diaspora Desk
